source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Curran_2000_RecreationalUsersNightAnd3Days.pdf, pp. 575–590 (all 16 pages). Text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout; all pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1–3, Figures 1–4 and the results text on pp. 580–585 checked on the rendered pages. The text layer is born-digital (only the fi/fl ligatures are lost) and every number used below matched the page image.

claims.overstatement: The headline 'people who use ketamine less often did not score lower' is stated without qualification, but this study's ketamine group used ketamine from twice a week to once a month (p. 580), i.e. at the frequency the claim calls 'less often', and it scored lower than peers with little or no ketamine use on story recall, category naming and sentence judging 3 days after a night of use, inside the claim's one-to-seven-day window. The claim's sentence on this study does not say how often its ketamine group used. No causal overstatement: the claim keeps causation open, as the authors do (p. 587).
claims.note: The two numbers taken from this study reproduce from Table 1 (day 3 category fluency 14.85 against 19.68; immediate story recall 7.75 against 10.18). Parts not supported as worded: (1) the frequency of use of this ketamine group (above); (2) the claim applies the missed-practice explanation only to story recall, but the authors' own check (ketamine group on day 3 against controls on day 0) was also non-significant for category naming (p. 584; editors' recalculation from Table 1: t(37) = 2.07, p = 0.046, above the paper's alpha of 0.01), and Curran & Morgan themselves already attributed the day-3 recall deficit to lack of practice (p. 586), not only the later study's authors; (3) time since last use: no ketamine on days 1–3, but 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after the day-0 testing, and all participants used alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1–2 (p. 580). The groups were matched for education here (15 of 20 and 18 of 19 at university level, p. 579), unlike the later comparisons. The day-3 difference the authors treat as most robust, sentence judging (63.30 against 79.11), is not mentioned in this claim.

anchors.locator: Results › Reported drug use on day 0 (end) and Reported general drug use
anchors.extracted: Ketamine group's usual frequency: 12% twice a week, 29% once a week, 47% once every 2 weeks, 12% once a month (sums to 100%; about 3.2 to 3.4 uses a month, editors' calculation; the same team later gives 3.1 a month, Curran & Monaghan 2001 p. 758); 35% had used for under 1 year, 47% for 1–2 years, 18% for over 2 years. 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after the day-0 testing but none on days 1–3; all participants used alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1 and 2, none on day 3. claims.overstatement: None in the sentence on this study. The headline's 'dissociation in everyday life' and 'delusion-like beliefs' do not describe this study's measures: both scales were state ratings ('at this moment'), taken 3 days after a night of use, and the schizotypal questionnaire was built for the study and not validated (pp. 579, 587).
claims.note: Every number taken from this study reproduces from Table 2 (day 3 dissociation 17.75 against 5.37; schizotypal 62.35 against 26.42; HADS depression 4.45 against 1.89 on day 0 and 4.30 against 1.68 on day 3). The frequency range (twice a week to once a month) is right (p. 580). The day-3 differences were significant post hoc (dissociation p<0.008, schizotypy p<0.001, p. 584; recomputed t-tests p = 0.007 and p<0.001). 'Slightly higher depression' matches the authors (p. 587); levels were well below the 8–11 range they call clinically significant (p. 585). The HADS analysis has df (1,32), so only about 34 of the 39 contributed. Reporting point: both scales are described as rated from 1 to 5 (p. 579), but totals below the number of items (controls 5.37 on 19 items; 26.42 on 30 items) imply 0–4 scoring.

anchors.extracted: The schizotypy questionnaire was devised for this study, reliable but not validated, and taps psychosis proneness rather than clinical psychoticism; the authors say their data cannot separate cumulative effects, residual effects and pre-existing differences for the day-3 dissociation and schizotypy differences.

claims.overstatement: Two places. (1) 'Three days later, at home and by their own account without ketamine in between' is not right for this study: 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after the day-0 testing (none on days 1–3), and all participants used alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1–2 (p. 580). (2) The opening sentence says most differences had gone by day 3 and only some memory differences remained; in this study dissociation and schizotypal scores also stayed significantly higher on day 3 (p. 584), which the claim states only later. Otherwise the wording is association-only and the numbers justify 'much lower' (standardized differences about 1 to 2).
claims.note: All numbers taken from this study reproduce from Tables 1–3 and pp. 579–585. Editors' calculations: (a) standardized differences on day 0 for the seven tests listed: Cohen's d 0.96 (cancellation time) to 2.01 (immediate recall), Hedges' g 0.94 to 1.97; 'about 0.9 to 2.0' reproduces with g, 'about 1.0 to 2.0' with d. (b) Sentence-judging practice check (ketamine day 3, 63.30 (16.04), n = 20, against controls day 0, 76.05 (21.45), n = 19): t(37) = 2.11, p = 0.042 (Welch p = 0.044), not the printed p<0.009; same result as the claim. Further qualifications: the same check for category naming gave no significant difference (p. 584; recalculated p = 0.046), so at the paper's alpha of 0.01 neither category naming nor sentence judging is separated from missed practice; 'judged ... sentences' should be 'correctly judged'; 'mostly also smoked cannabis' = all 20 of the ketamine group and 17 of 19 controls; amounts were self-reported (printed pp. 579–580), not tested; blinding of testers is not reported (the ketamine group was defined at recruitment). Reporting point: Table 2 mood 'alertness' factor 59.37 against 47.27 on day 0 and 37.59 against 38.89 on day 3 implies a group difference on the night (recomputed t(37) = 2.93, p = 0.006) and a large fall across days, yet the text reports only a trend for day on contentedness (p. 585), so 'mood changed little' rests on the text, not the table.

anchors.extracted: All 20 of the ketamine group and 17 controls smoked cannabis on day 0; alcohol on day 0 by 72% of controls and 65% of the ketamine group (more than 2 hours before testing); two ketamine and one control had a quarter MDMA tablet over 4 hours before; 36% of the ketamine group took ketamine after the day-0 testing but none on days 1–3; all participants used alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1–2, none on day 3. risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall for any causal reading of the day-3 differences, and high rather than very high for the day-0 contrast, as the card reasons. My step-1 note followed the authors in calling the groups matched for education; the card's 75% against 95% (Fisher p = 0.18) is the better description.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The gaps listed (practice check that does not reproduce, imperfect matching, no norms, trait-like self-rating scales, dose comparison without purity or route) all check against the pages.

missed: Letter fluency: the paper's own tests reached only trend level at its alpha of 0.01 (group F(1,37) = 6.0, p = 0.019; group x day F(1,37) = 4.4, p = 0.04; p. 583), yet the Discussion lists letter fluency among the tasks very markedly impaired on the night (p. 585). Key finding 5 and the interpretation gap present it as an acute deficit without this caveat (the table difference itself is large, g about -1.04).

Day-3 dissociation in the ketamine group has an SD about equal to its mean (17.75, SD 17.41; Table 2, p. 581), a skewed distribution in which a few people may carry the day-3 group difference; with n = 20 the parametric post hoc test (p<0.008, p. 584) should be read with that in mind.
